BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Come late weekend, another strong upper-level low pressure system from off the upper Pacific coast will weaken as it moves onshore into the northwest region.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Cool and unsettled pattern will continue periods of valley rain and accumulating mountain snow today through Friday.
- Return of unsettled patterns with precipitation chances Sunday through late next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The closed upper low will center over our area today as it steers eastward as a longwave trough through the end of the week. Strong southerly flow ahead of the low center will continue steering abundant moisture over the area today through Friday. Rain showers will be more dispersed and much lower in coverage for lower elevations today. Mountains should see continuous snow showers thanks to the orographic lifting enhancements provided by the southerly flow. The strong southerly will also bring slightly warmer daytime temperatures and higher snow levels up to 4.5-5.5 kft MSL today, making rain the dominant precip type for lower elevations come early afternoon. As the low center passes directly over our area later today, a strong plume of moisture will return more continuous rain over valley areas tonight through Friday morning. This moisture plume will also likely bring heavier snowfall across Malheur and Owyhee counties in the southern portions of our CWA. Precipitation tapers off from west to east in the valleys on Friday as the low exits the area. Mountains hold onto snow showers through the day, but any additional accumulation will be very limited and generally less than an inch. By late Friday, higher terrain areas will have seen 3 to 5 inches of total snowfall from this system, with up to 10 inches in higher peaks. Cooler temperatures and gusty northwest winds expected Friday as the area comes under the drier backend of the trough. A brief upper ridge will build into the region Saturday, keeping the area dry but barely warmer. Temperatures will stay near normal through the weekend.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Come late weekend, another strong upper-level low pressure system from off the upper Pacific coast will weaken as it moves onshore into the northwest region. This weakening system will steer a shortwave trough across our area, returning precipitation chances early Sunday. There remains good guidance agreement on the precipitation coverage remaining highly limited and short-lived over the more northwest portions of our area. Snow levels will hover below valley floors through most of Sunday. The Treasure Valley will see around a 10-20% chance of a rain/snow mix in the early morning hours of Sunday. Mountains in the northern half of our CWA will see a 40-60% chance of snow showers continuing through late Sunday. Another weak embedded shortwave trough will dig across the upper Great Basin through early Monday, bringing a 15-30% chance of light snow showers over the easternmost portions of our CWA Monday morning. Late Monday through Tuesday, an amplified ridge of high pressure will build into the area and return drier conditions and a slight warming trend. Late Tuesday through Thursday, there is considerable guidance uncertainty over the trajectory of another strong Pacific upper low moving into the region. It can either remain quasi-stationary off the coast of British Columbia and drive an eastward-moving swath of precipitation over our area from Tuesday through Thursday, or dig directly south of our area into the Great Basin and bring very limited precipitation chances through the week. For now, the long-term guidance projects next Wednesday through Thursday to remain unsettled with moderate to high precipitation chances returning areawide.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: A fairly active pattern also looks likely to continue next week, with trough working through the region every few days. This means there's chance for additional mountain snow Monday into Tuesday, and again sometime late week next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Next storm system arrives Friday, bringing chances for mountain snow through Saturday.
- Gusty winds and elevated fire weather conditions on Friday across most of the Front Range foothills and plains.
- Cooler pattern emerges this weekend into next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: The flow aloft will increase on Friday ahead of another trough axis. This also looks to be the last warm day before a cooler pattern takes over for the weekend into next week, with highs reaching the upper 50s to low 60s. 700mb flow reaches about 40kt by midday Friday in a broadly subsident regime, meaning that widespread wind gusts are expected to develop across the Front Range and plains during the afternoon. For the lower elevations, elevated fire weather conditions will again be a concern in this pattern. Two limiting factors are (1) the northern I-25 corridor often ends up at least partially sheltered in SW flow, and (2) relative humidity looks to be at least a little bit higher than Wednesday.

Across the mountains, moisture will begin to increase during the morning hours, leading to a gradual increase in snow. With a ~120kt jet streak remaining nearly stationary over northwestern Colorado, one dominant band of light (to at times moderate) snow somewhere over northern Colorado, with weaker orographic snow showers across the rest of the mountains. Overall moisture is still somewhat limited, and there may be a break in between shortwaves Friday afternoon into Friday night.

A second shortwave is expected to track through the state on Saturday. There's enough moisture for another organized round of light snow, this time focused along and south of the I-70 mountains. Snowfall totals in this period will again be on the light side. Guidance continues to struggle with the evolution of this shortwave as is tracks into southwestern Kansas during the day. Several deterministic models (e.g., ECMWF, RGEM) are insistent that a band of snow will spread into the Denver metro and/or Palmer Divide during the morning hours Saturday, with generally light (roughly a half inch to inch) snowfall amounts possible. On the other hand, the GFS and most of the American short term/regional guidance is weaker with the developing surface low over the OK panhandle and struggle to produce any QPF outside of the higher terrain. I have a slight preference towards the ECMWF solution in this time period and our grids are close to the previous forecast - which is higher than the current NBM.

This system will also usher in a period of cooler weather across the forecast area. Even between systems Sunday and Monday, temperatures across the plains will likely settle in the mid to upper 40s. Guidance is in good agreement that near to below normal temperatures will continue through the rest of the forecast period with highs sticking in the 40s.

A fairly active pattern also looks likely to continue next week, with trough working through the region every few days. This means there's chance for additional mountain snow Monday into Tuesday, and again sometime late week next week. What system brings the best chance at snow to the region? It's difficult to say. Deterministic solutions continue to swing wildly from run to run in this period. As we've seen with this upcoming Friday/Saturday system, this pattern continues to have low predictability, and large day-to-day/run-to-run swings are likely to continue through most of the upcoming forecast period.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: The storm track will remain active into next week, with several upper level shortwave troughs continuing to move inland off of the Pacific.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Locally heavy snow showers will return to Carbon County and portions of Albany/Converse Counties Thursday night into Friday morning.
- Another round of strong, gusty winds is expected Friday into Friday night, producing elevated fire weather conditions over the High Plains.
- Expect chillier temperatures this weekend into early next week with a few additional chances for light, spotty snow showers.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Transient ridging aloft is moving across the area today in the wake of yesterday's storm system. However, the next weather system is already on our doorstep, with GOES water vapor channel imagery showing plenty of mid to high cloud cover beginning to encroach from the west ahead of the sprawling closed low spinning over northern California. At the surface, high pressure settling in over the High Plains is expected to keep winds lighter today. However, southwest flow aloft will keep breezy to windy conditions going to the west, mainly in Carbon county. Extremely dry air (PW near or even less than 0.1") lingers behind yesterday's event, and is currently centered over Albany county. Dewpoints below 0F are still showing up this morning! As temperatures warm in response to the weak ridging aloft, we will see very low humidity develop in Albany county, spilling into neighboring counties as well. Fortunately, the strongest winds are not expected to be collocated with the lowest humidity today, but elevated fire weather conditions can be anticipated in these areas. We should see moisture advection both from the west and the east today, but it will take some time to erode this bone-dry airmass.

Mid to upper level moisture will improve from the west rapidly this evening as the next storm system nears. Moist southwest orographic lift should initiate another round of snow showers in Carbon county this evening. This activity will be widely scattered to begin with, but expect coverage to increase after midnight as the lower atmosphere approaches saturation. Forecast soundings show some decent (for November) convective instability in place in Carbon county overnight and Friday morning, on the order of a few hundred J/kg of CAPE. Low to mid-level lapse rates are also very steep for this time of year. Thus, expect this snow activity to be showery in nature, with potential for locally heavy snow and even snow squalls. The primary window appears to be 3AM to noon on Friday. Due to the convective character, accumulations may be somewhat hit-or-miss. Areas that get under bands of heavier snow could easily pick up 1 to 3" of snow even in the lower elevations of the county. The higher peaks could pick up 6+" under brief, heavier snowfall rates, but confidence was not quite high enough that this will be consistent and/or widespread to issue a Winter Weather Advisory just yet. Models are in fairly good agreement showing drier air moving in by midday Friday. This probably won't completely shut off snow shower activity, but expect coverage and rates to decrease considerably.

Winds will be on the increase through the day on Friday as southwest flow aloft increases ahead of the next trough axis, which should arrive in the afternoon or evening hours. Winds do not look nearly as strong as yesterday's event, but we still have 700-mb winds around 35 to 45 knots over southeast Wyoming per model consensus. Most of the area can expect another windy day, with widespread gusts of 35 to 55 mph across the area. Marginally high winds are possible in the typical gap wind areas, with in-house guidance showing about a 40% chance for high winds at most of these gaps. Typical parameters such as height/pressure gradients across the barrier are just short of what we would typically look for to issue high wind headlines, so held off for now, but will need to watch this as we are quite close. Friday's temperatures should remain mild over most of the High Plains, supporting elevated fire weather conditions along and south of the North Platte River Valley. Colder air is expected west of the Laramie Range.

The first axis of a highly disorganized upper level system will pass through Friday evening, but numerous other vort-maxes will linger over the area behind. Additional light snow shower activity will continue Friday afternoon and evening, possibly spreading into Converse and Niobrara counties. Little to no precipitation is expected east of I-25 and south of US-20, but areas north and west of there may be able to pick up a dusting to an inch or so by Saturday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Chilly and unsettled weather will linger through the weekend, as models are in fairly good agreement showing that ridging will not immediately fill back in over the area this time. The flow aloft remains zonal-ish, with a chilly surface high over the northern Plains preventing us from realizing a small increase in 700-mb temperatures on Sunday. A few isolated snow showers will be possible both Saturday and Sunday, but QPF expectations are minimal. Mostly, it will actually feel like November for a change, with highs in the upper 30s to lower 40s to most. This will actually be a few degrees colder than seasonal averages.

The storm track will remain active into next week, with several upper level shortwave troughs continuing to move inland off of the Pacific. However, nearly all ensembles continue to show these systems falling apart by the time they reach our area, and thus there is not really a clear signal for notable snowfall anytime soon. The next trough will arrive around the Monday to Tuesday time frame, and may bring some light snow to portions of the area, though a quarter of ensemble members are completely dry. Confidence is higher that it will at least reinforce the chilly air, such that Monday and Tuesday are expected to be the coldest days of the week. Temperatures should recover somewhat on Wednesday and Thursday (Thanksgiving Day), but we should still be fairly close to seasonal averages. Another upper level trough may traverse the Rockies around Thanksgiving, but at least 50% of ensemble members bring this one through completely dry as well.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Unsettled weather will return to the region during Thanksgiving week, though specific timing and track details remain uncertain. Even so, a series of disturbances propagating through the area will likely bring minor travel impacts to the mountains.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Measurable snowfall is expected Thursday night into Saturday for the mountains, with some high valleys also seeing light accumulations.
- Temperatures will trend downward for the weekend, with most desert valleys seeing their first freezing temperatures of the year.
- Fast moving storms are possible through much of Thanksgiving week. Stay tuned for updates to timing and impacts as they become available.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: An upstream cyclone continues moving onshore into the Pacific Northwest today, with its associated moisture streaming into the Intermountain West this afternoon on strong southerly flow aloft. This moisture plume will reach our western CWA by late afternoon as the nose of the jet pushes into the region, aligning along an axis from southeast Utah to the northern mountains by Thursday nightfall. Current high-resolution guidance indicates weak instability accompanying this system, which will likely result in streaky, banded precipitation. Due to this convective nature, confidence remains low regarding widespread or prolonged impacts.

That said, there remains a roughly 70% probability of 4 to 6 inches of snow across the higher elevations of the Elk, West Elk, Flat Tops, and Park ranges. The eastern Uintas will see a slightly higher ceiling, with a ~70% chance of 4 to 8 inches due to a longer duration of snowfall compared to surrounding areas. Across the open travel corridors, expected accumulations are lower, and hazardous travel impacts remain uncertain. Meanwhile, persistent moist southerly flow across the southern mountains will keep light flurries lingering over the highest peaks, though the deepest moisture will exit the region before the main axis of instability shifts east Friday afternoon.

Wind will be an additional concern during this forecast period. As the jet noses into the region, gusty winds will develop today and persist into Friday, with gusts reaching up to 45 mph in spots, particularly across higher elevations. Combined with falling or fresh snow, these gusts could produce localized areas of blowing snow and reduced visibility.

By Saturday, a trailing lobe of energy will rotate through the Great Basin toward the Four Corners. Although deep moisture will be largely scoured out by this point, dynamic forcing and increasing snow ratios could still trigger a brief burst of heavier snowfall rates over the southern mountains. Because this wave will be relatively fast-moving, accumulations over the southern mountains should generally remain around 3 to 6 inches. Temperatures will also trend colder behind this system this weekend, bringing single-digit lows to higher elevations.

Unsettled weather will return to the region during Thanksgiving week, though specific timing and track details remain uncertain. Even so, a series of disturbances propagating through the area will likely bring minor travel impacts to the mountains. Continue to monitor the latest forecasts as model consensus improves on the timing of these waves. Daily highs and lows will also trend roughly 5 degrees below seasonal normals.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Temperatures will remain below normal for Sunday into next week with the active weather pattern continuing as a parade of upper troughs move through westerly flow aloft.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Potential for high winds across southern Sangres and wind prone areas of the southern I-25 corridor Thursday night through mid day Friday.
- Windy and warm again for Friday with elevated fire weather conditions possible for portions of the I-25 corridor and adjacent plains.
- A couple rounds of light snow for the Continental Divide Thursday night through mid day Saturday with low chances showers to spill eastward across the adjacent plains on Saturday.
- Remaining unsettled with below normal temperatures into next week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Another mild day expected today with less wind across most of southern CO. After a cold start to the morning, temperatures will rebound back into the 50s to mid 60s across the valleys and plains with 30s and 40s for the high country.

Winds will start to increase again across the high country as the next upper low moves into the Pacific Northwest today before translating eastward into the Great Basin by later tonight. This puts southern CO under increasing southwest flow aloft especially into tonight. Orographically enhanced snow showers will spread into the Continental Divide tonight with some light snow accumulations possible across the Eastern San Juans. Areas of blowing and drifting snow across the higher areas will be likely as winds gusts up to 60 mph towards dawn. Moisture looks insufficient to produce snow for the Sangre De Cristo mountains through Friday, but winds will increase across the peaks with HRRR, RFFS, and REFs suggesting the potential for mountain wave high winds across the eastern slopes of the southern Sangre De Cristos and portions of the southern I-25 corridor from roughly 11 PM Thu through 11 AM Friday. Peak period for the strongest gusts maximizes between around 11-16z as a mountain top stable layer develops and flow aloft attains some weak reverse shear. Forward shear increases Friday afternoon but deep mixing may still hang on to some localized near high wind criteria for the lower elevation zones. Probabilities off REFs and NBM suggest a localized 50-80% chance for high winds across western portions of Huerfano county and the eastern slopes of the southern Sangre De Cristo zone, so will go out with a high wind watch for these areas.

As for snow accumulations, amounts in the 1 to 3 inch range will be possible along the Continental Divide, particularly for eastern San Juans and Sawatch range. There will be areas of blowing and drifting snow as southwest winds gust up to 60 mph by Friday morning. But overall, impacts may be limited due to the light amounts, and no winter weather highlights appear necessary. The San Luis Valley could also see some near high wind criteria gusts on Friday but confidence is lower for this area.

For the remainder of southern CO, it will be dry and windy, with elevated fire weather conditions possible for portions of the I-25 corridor as humidity values drop to around 20 percent and winds gust up to 40 to 50 mph. Area of greatest concern will be El Paso county, though given the marginal nature of minimum humidity readings, no fire weather highlights are anticipated at this time.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Trailing energy drops into the 4 corners region Friday night keeping some light snow showers going across the southwest mountains before the system moves across CO on Saturday as an open wave of varying amplitudes. Overall, moisture appears lacking and any precipitation may be brief, spotty and light across the southeast plains, if it happens at all, on Saturday. The Palmer Divide and Raton ridge could see some light snow, though any accumulations would be brief and confined to the grassy and cold surfaces.

The system pulls away to the east Saturday night with a chilly night expected into Sunday morning. Lows may drop into the single digits across some of the mountains/valley locations, with 20s across the lower elevations.

Temperatures will remain below normal for Sunday into next week with the active weather pattern continuing as a parade of upper troughs move through westerly flow aloft. Sunday will be dry, but snow showers could return to portions of the area later Monday into Tuesday. There is low confidence on these details as the system looks pretty open and progressive in the 00z operational runs. But this could change with future runs. Another storm system is expected for late week with even greater uncertainty on timing, strength and track.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: With no blocking ridge developing off the Pacific coast, this break in the action will be short lived, with increasing confidence that an active pattern will persist for much of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A Pacific Northwest storm system will bring periods of snow to Utah's mountains through early Saturday, increasingly focused over northern Utah as time goes on. Significant snow accumulations will bring travel difficulties to high elevations routes. Snow levels will drop to northern Utah valley floors Friday night, bringing a chance of accumulating snow.
- Freezing temperatures are increasing in probability for the Virgin River corridor near Zion National Park Saturday and Sunday mornings.

- Dry conditions are expected over the weekend before a weaker system impacts primarily southern Utah Monday into Tuesday. An active pattern is expected to continue for the remainder of the upcoming week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A broad trough currently is currently centered over the Pacific Northwest, with the associated frontal boundary over eastern Nevada this morning. In moisture and instability on the leading edge of the system, precipitation has already begun over the western half of Utah, with snow levels in the 5500-6500 foot range. Thus, mountain snow is already accumulating. This system will come through Utah and southwest Wyoming in pieces through early Saturday.

Light and steady precipitation is expected to continue during the day today, with a burst of heavier valley rain/mountain snow tonight into early Friday as the frontal boundary crosses the area. Behind the front, precip will become primarily focused over northern Utah where the best cold pool instability will remain. As the main trough tracks across the area, temperatures and thus snow levels will steadily lower during the day Friday, bringing snow levels down to northern Utah valley floors late Friday into early Saturday, bringing the potential for accumulating snow. Limiting factor on those accumulations will be the duration of precipitation after snow levels lower sufficiently and that rates will be generally lower during this time.

Overall, guidance has been trending upward with snowfall totals over the last several runs, particularly over northern Utah. With two feet of snow now in the forecast for portions of the Wasatch including the Upper Cottonwoods, have upgraded both the northern and southern Wasatch mountain zones to a Winter Storm Warning given anticipated impacts with other headlines unchanged at this time.

Behind the exit trough, confidence is high that high pressure will track across Utah and southwest Wyoming Saturday into Sunday, bringing dry conditions. With the clearing and unseasonably cool airmass, freezing temperatures will be in play for lower elevation portions of southern Utah, with the best chance in the Virgin River corridor of Zion National Park. This remains more likely Friday night/Saturday morning than on Sunday morning. Temperatures in the vicinity of St. George are also expected to get close to freezing, though there is a relatively low chance of temperatures moving to or below freezing overnight during that period.

With no blocking ridge developing off the Pacific coast, this break in the action will be short lived, with increasing confidence that an active pattern will persist for much of the upcoming week. The next storm system is expected to move through Monday into Tuesday. Latest guidance is leaning toward a solution that is noticeably weaker than the last couple of systems, bringing minor impacts to primarily southern Utah. Beyond that, there is the potential for a stronger system to move through for the middle to latter part of next week.

2660.travel_advice: Heightened avalanche conditions on specific terrain features. Evaluate snow and terrain carefully; identify features of concern.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Recent wind-drifted snow will keep the avalanche danger elevated near and above treeline on slopes facing west through north to east. Small avalanches will be easy to trigger, especially just below ridgelines. Steer clear of steep slopes if you feel wind-stiffened snow or see shooting cracks as you travel.
Below treeline conditions are generally safe due to thin or non-existent snow cover.

2745.travel_advice: Generally safe avalanche conditions. Watch for unstable snow on isolated terrain features.

product.author: Ian Fowler
bottom_line: Most slopes are safe and lack sufficient coverage for an avalanche. At high elevations, steer clear of isolated patches of firm, drifted snow below ridges or in steep gullies.

3046.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

3014.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Kevin Studley
bottom_line: Winter has begun to embrace the West Central Mountains of Idaho. 6-12 inches of new snow has fallen between Friday the 13th and Monday the 16th. Another 6-12 inches could stack up by the end of the week. If you're traveling in the mountains this week, watch out for wind slabs 1-2 feet thick above 7,000 feet and pay attention to terrain traps.
We'll update the General Avalanche Information weekly until full-time forecasting operations begin.
hazard_discussion: From 60-degree temperatures to over a foot of new snow, the weather sure has changed quickly over the past week. A cooler and wetter weather pattern has taken shape over our region since Friday the 13th. As of Monday (16th) afternoon, some mountain locations have picked up 6-12 inches of new snow along with southerly winds gusting 20-30 MPH.
Wind Slabs
• Wind slabs could become reactive this week with over a foot of new snow and gusty winds. Wind slabs will be most sensitive just below ridgelines.
• Look for clues of wind-affected snow, such as drifts, dunes, pillows, and freshly built cornices.
• Watch for signs of instability, such as shooting cracks. If you're observing these signs, find another aspect away from wind-drifted snow.
• Strong winds and local terrain features can alter the prevailing wind direction. Pay attention to cross-loading and wind-loading on unsuspecting slopes.
Early Season Conditions
• If you're out hiking or hunting in the mountains this fall, stay tuned to changing weather conditions. Avalanches are most likely during and immediately after a storm.

• Keep in mind the adage, "If there's enough snow to ride, there's enough snow to slide". Even if there's not enough snow to bury you, a small slide over uncovered logs, rocks, and brush would not be a fun way to start the season.
• Stay up to date on mountain weather with our WEATHER tab, where you'll find webcams, weather stations, and weather forecasting tools.
Check Your Winter Gear

• Beacons, shovels, probes, airbags. Run through all your gear and make sure it's functioning properly. Does your transceiver or airbag need any firmware updates? Look for cracks, defects, or corroded batteries. Make it fun with your friends and do a pre-season gear check with your winter travel companions.
Continuing Education
• Check out the Education tab on our website to sign up for avalanche courses this winter (COURSES ).
• Stay tuned to our EVENTS pages for other local happenings with the winter community.
• Interested in attending a snow and avalanche workshop (SAW)? Check out A3's WEBSITE for a list of events.
Observations
• Keep an eye on our observation page HERE

• If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation HERE. Early season observations help forecasters and the public alike. A simple photo and/or weather observation helps paint the picture of where snow is and where it is not.

Yeah, that's right: the Payette Avalanche Center has a new website. Browse around before the snow starts flying. We're also on the Avy App. You can search for "Avy: Avalanche & Weather Info" in your app store on your mobile device.

product.author: Mike Walter
bottom_line: Recent winds created pockets of drifted snow at higher elevations. These pockets are isolated but could produce small avalanches. Assess high-elevation steep slopes before committing.
